newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Herzog in Budapest faces Holocaust survivors.
newsitem.headline: Herzog in Budapest faces Holocaust survivors.

text.p: A group of around 100 Holocaust survivors staged a protest for compensation as German President Roman Herzog visited Budapest's main synagogue on Tuesday.
As he arrived at the synagogue, the largest in Europe, a grim-faced Herzog inmmediately went over to the protesters who stood quietly behind barriers.

"He promised he would compensate us in the future along with the Czechs, Poles and Ukrainians," 73-year-old Magdolna Gottfried, who was deported from the eastern Hungarian town of Ozd in June 1944, told Reuters. "He was serious and correct. I believe him."
The protesters dispersed as soon as Herzog went in to the synagogue and the adjoining Holocaust museum, where he spent about an hour.
Another protester, Helen Fecher, 73, who spent one and a half years in Nazi death camps, expressed frustration that the process of compensation was taking so long.
"There are so few of us left the longer they take the less they have to pay," she said. "They're paying their retired people plenty but we get nothing."

Bonn signed last month a landmark joint post-war act of contrition with the Czech Republic, drawn up after two years of delicate talks, in which Germany expresses its sorrow for the Nazi occupation of the Czech lands between 1938 and 1945.
Prague expressed its regret for Czech brutality in the post-war expulsion of ethnic Sudeten Germans.
No such agreement exists with Hungary which was a German ally throughout World War Two.

In a three-day visit beginning on Tuesday and dominated by the issue of the treatment of minorities, Herzog earlier told Hungary he was sure it would be one of the first new members of the European Union.

"Hungary will enjoy the support of Germany for its integration into European Union and NATO," Herzog said in a speech to Hungary's parliament. "I am sure Hungary will be one of the first candidates to be admitted to the EU and NATO."
Herzog said he was impressed by the perseverance Hungary had shown in its efforts towards European integration and described its legislation on minority rights as exemplary.
"An unmistakeable sign of the maturity of the new Hungarian democracy is the way Hungary treats its minorities," he said. "The legislation can serve as a model for the whole of eastern Europe."

Hungary was one of the first post-communist states of central and eastern Europe to adopt Council of Europe legisalative norms for the protection of language education and cultural and political rights for ethnic minorities in the country.
On Wednesday Herzog will visit the German-speaking Schwab community in the village of Solymar, near Budapest, and hold talks with leaders of Hungary's other ethnic minorities.
Herzog made a specific appeal in his speech to Parliament for Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to be allowed to become an integral part of Europe.
"Europe cannot be complete unless Budapest, Prague and Warsaw belong to it as well -- this is not a romantic dream but the imperative of reality," he said.
